citations.sentence: This week's feature reports that "anxiety" was one of the most-searched words in a popular Bible app this year [[1]].
YouVersion says "anxiety," "hope" and "healing" were among the most-searched terms in its Bible App this year, and that "Psalm 91" was the single most-searched term of all [[1]].
The ministry released the data on Oct 6 [[1]].
The release reports that daily use reached 18.5 million people, up more than 13% from 2025 [[1]].
Every figure in this story is self-reported by YouVersion. No outside group has audited them, and the release does not define "daily use" or explain how search terms were counted.
citations.note: Attributed absence from dossier sections 2 and Unverified/gaps (methodology gap; no independent coverage found). Checkable against source 1. Caller instruction: say figures are self-reported.

citations.sentence: Psalm 91 is a psalm of trust in God as refuge and shelter, so its place at the top fits the other searches.
citations.note: Description of Scripture content (dossier section 4: 'Psalm 91 as refuge'); not quoted text.

citations.sentence: YouVersion's 2025 data listed love, anxiety and peace among the most-searched terms, and named Isaiah 41:10, where God tells his people not to fear, as the most engaged-with verse [[2]].
"This year, we've been encouraged by how many people are turning to Scripture for answers to their questions," said Bobby Gruenewald, YouVersion's founder and CEO [[1]].
YouVersion is a digital ministry of Life.Church, and its Bible apps are free [[1]].
Its Family of Apps offers 3,800 versions of the Bible in 2,400 languages, and it works with more than 45,000 churches and partners [[1]].
After passing one billion installs last November, it added more than 160 million new installs in 2026, the company says [[1]].
Participants are encouraged to read every day, "whether through a favorite print Bible or digitally through an app" [[1]].
YouVersion says nearly 3 million people signed up for the Challenge's first year in 2025 [[1]].
This year the Challenge adds a feature that lets users "track their progress and see how their friends are engaging alongside them" [[1]].
That sign-up figure should not be set beside last year's report, which said "more than 2.6 million people took" the Challenge [[2]].
Its 2025 record day had "more than 19 million people opening the app in a single day" [[2]].
YouVersion's privacy policy lists "search history" among the information it collects [[3]].
The company says it does not sell or share personal data with third-party advertisers, and that it publishes engagement stats only "in an aggregated form" [[3]].

A 2013 essay from the University of Chicago Divinity School's Sightings argued that, with YouVersion, engagement with religious content is being shaped by "the same methods advertisers use to compel us to buy and consume their products" [[4]].
Ascension has released the Catholic Reading Bible: Dyslexia-Friendly Edition, which it calls "the first complete Catholic Bible to feature the Grace typeface" [[5]].

Ascension says Grace was developed by the Bible design firm 2K/DENMARK, "informed by research, testing with dyslexic readers, and work involving the University of Cambridge," and that the design uses lines of no more than 35 characters, ragged-right text and 11-point type [[5]].
Christianity Today reported in 2024 that Grace was first used in Bibles from Lifeway and Crossway, and that its designer made the font nonproprietary [[6]].
One caveat: research on earlier dyslexia fonts has found little evidence that they help people read faster or more accurately [[7]], and we found no published peer-reviewed results for Grace itself.

Gloo's AI Hackathon gave its Best of Bible Track award, powered by YouVersion, to Envoy Mission, which Gloo describes as an offline, private Bible delivered through multilingual AI conversations with seekers [[8]].
Track winners received $20,000 each, from a field of more than 1,000 builders on more than 115 teams [[8]].
Envoy Mission is a hackathon prototype, and Gloo's release is the only public description of it we found.
citations.note: Dossier Gloo section: single source, no independent page found; treat as prototype (caller instruction).

citations.sentence: On Oct 6, Pray.com launched Pray Production Studio, an AI tool that turns a sermon into cinematic video, with plans starting at $19 a month [[9]].

In 2025, Jeffrey Bilbro, an English professor at Grove City College, told NPR that the company's AI Bible videos situate the Bible "as entertainment, as content to be titillated or amused by," rather than "a word that is a divine revelation intended to transform our lives" [[10]].
Brad East of Abilene Christian University said the videos rob the Bible of its power by reducing it to an action movie [[10]].
